claim: FBS gives a small vocabulary of six variables (R, F, Be, Bs, S, D) and eight named processes (formulation, synthesis, analysis, evaluation, documentation, reformulation I-III) that has been used to code designers' protocols; its completeness has been debated, and later work extends it (a ninth F-to-S process for fast thinking; 20 processes in the situated version).
agent_test: Add explicit F/Be/Bs/S tags to scratch state; compare tagged vs untagged traces at equal tokens on design/planning tasks.
audit_note: Eight processes and six variables match Gero's FBS, but no source says it can code any design protocol: completeness has been debated (Galle, Dorst and Vermaas, Ralph), the situated version uses 20 processes, and Kannengiesser and Gero (2019) add a ninth process (F to S) for System 1.
claim_before_audit: FBS gives a small, closed state vocabulary (R, F, Be, Bs, S, D) and eight named transitions (formulation, synthesis, analysis, evaluation, documentation, reformulation I-III) that can code any design protocol.

claim: The FBS scheme has been applied to individual, team, student, professional and remote designers in several domains (over 10,000 coded hours), but the evidence for domain independence is mostly figures and cumulative-occurrence curves, not strong inferential tests.
agent_test: Run the same coding on agent traces over code, math and design tasks; check whether the process profile is stable.
audit_note: All sources are from Gero's own group (Gero/Kan/Pourmohamadi, Kannengiesser/Gero, Gero/Milovanovic); the 10,000 coded hours are one domain (industrial systems design, Bott and Mesmer 2019) reported second-hand; and the Kannengiesser-Gero paper simulates three published process models with ANOVAs that found a common slope only for function issues (p=0.06), so it does use inferential tests and mostly shows differences between domains.

claim: Pahl-Beitz systematic design does not predict real student FBS process profiles well: the model has a much lower Bs slope than empirical data, and F and Be are nonlinear in all datasets.
agent_test: Compare a fixed linear stage order against a free FBS-guided order at equal tokens.

claim: Expertise shows in how effort is spread, not in FBS process frequencies: decomposition is about 22% for engineers vs about 15% for freshmen and seniors (d up to 2.55, N=50), and professionals spend more at system level 1 (0.12 vs 0.06). Wells 2016 found no significant FBS difference between pre-engineering and other students (all p>0.05, N=40).
agent_test: Force a decompose-recompose pass vs none at equal tokens; measure solution quality.

claim: Sophomore design education changed FBS profiles only descriptively; no causal control beyond 3 controls and only year 1 reported.
agent_test: Not testable on an agent.

claim: FBS coding by LLM works only after rules are tuned: three human experts scored 54%, 93%, 87%; ChatGPT with rules about 78%, then 100% on the items it was tuned on; the held-out classifier scored 71% (n=31; F1 85 function, 57 behaviour, 64 structure). Nearest held-out analogue outside design (Dunivin 2024, 111 gold passages): GPT-4 kappa 0.68 per code with a rationale step vs 0.59 without; rare codes are the weakest.
agent_test: Test an LLM tagger against two human coders on held-out agent traces; require kappa above 0.7 before using tags.

claim: Behaviour is the hardest FBS category to classify reliably (F1 57 vs 85 for function, 64 for structure).
agent_test: Check whether behaviour tags on agent traces are unstable across runs.

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs are poor at domain-specific function classification (GPT-3.5 0.04, GPT-4 Turbo 0.27, GPT-4o mini 0.20) but fine-tuning on 10% of data reached 0.89 test accuracy; more data lowered accuracy (0.63 at 90%), so this is no clean scaling law. No second study reproducing the falling test accuracy was found (search limited).
agent_test: Shows tuning, not prompting, drove the gain; not a scaffold test.

claim: An FBS-structured knowledge graph helps failure-cause retrieval when evidence is sparse (precision 1.0 vs 0.50, recall 0.625 vs 0.375 at n=8) and gives no gain when matching records are plentiful.
agent_test: Store past solutions as F/B/S nodes vs free text; compare retrieval at equal tokens on hard, differently-worded cases.

claim: Prompting LLMs for concepts trades novelty against fit: few-shot raised similarity to crowd solutions (0.804) and lowered novelty (hull volume 0.2 vs crowd 0.294); zero-shot plus 'unique' gave 0.746. LLMs repeat solutions with slight edits.
agent_test: Compare few-shot-with-examples vs zero-shot with novelty cue on diversity at equal tokens.

claim: A critique-and-revise step gave the largest gain in LLM idea quality in a 4000-solution study, yet stayed below humans on novelty; LLM recall of known solutions was 1.00 vs human 0.25-0.80.
agent_test: Add one critique-revise pass; measure novelty and diversity gain per token.

claim: FBS-guided stage prompts changed diversity and novelty modestly and inconsistently across problems (DPP diversity front porch A 83.1, B 68.8, C 122.3, D 96.4; judge validity ICC from -0.52 to 0.72).
agent_test: Replicate F/B/S stage prompts on our tasks; check judge agreement first.

claim: A multi-agent LLM setup for conceptual systems engineering gave more nodes (about 6 vs 1-2.8) at much higher cost (about 650 s vs 39 s) and lower code compile rate (34.8% vs 100%); requirement coverage stayed at 20% or less.
agent_test: Compare single agent with FBS tags vs multi-agent at equal tokens.

claim: LLM designers imitate the spread of human design processes poorly: soundness averaged 0.298 for the LLM vs 0.42-0.495 for humans, with variance 0.042 vs 0.102.
agent_test: Measure variance of agent traces across seeds; narrow variance may signal mode collapse.

claim: Designers judge generative AI most useful for idea generation (86.7%) and problem definition (73.3%) and keep selection and evaluation human-led (86.7%).
agent_test: Not an agent test.

claim: Practitioners favour sensemaking-coevolution-implementation over rational-plan models (96.6% of 1384 respondents; p<0.001 on every item), supporting co-evolving problem and solution states.
agent_test: Let the agent revise requirements mid-run vs a fixed spec; compare on tasks with hidden requirements.
audit_note: Single study (Ralph 2013); 96.6% is share with median response agreeing with SCI; Kannengiesser & Zhu exists but is background only.

claim: An FBS prompt chain (requirements to function to behaviour to structure, with a human picking words at each hop) gave higher rated concept quality than free ChatGPT prompting: 3.31 vs 2.90 (weighted, 5-point scale; 80 participants, 20 per group; 3 raters, Fleiss kappa 0.66). The reported t-tests look inflated (t 6.64 implies about 60 scores per group, not 20 concepts), and professionals gained almost nothing over free prompting (0.02).
agent_test: Same stage chain with code, not a human, choosing what moves forward; compare to free prompting at equal tokens.

claim: The FBS scaffold's benefit appears larger for novices than for professionals (novice gain 0.51 and 0.68 over two controls; professional gain 0.37 and 0.02), so a scaffold's gain may shrink as base skill rises.
agent_test: Run the FBS chain on a weak and a strong model; check whether the gain shrinks.

claim: Maher and Poon's co-evolution model is an algorithm (two evolving populations, problem and solution, with a fitness check that triggers refocus) later used descriptively for human design; no replication numbers for the original were found. Under FBS, co-evolution can be measured as reciprocal first-occurrence changes, and attention-switch counts overstate it (by about 50% and about 100% in one 1-hour session).
agent_test: Log new problem items and new solution items in agent traces; count reciprocal triggers, not mode switches.

claim: In an FBS-coded team session, most co-evolution was between behaviour and structure and was nearly continuous; function-structure links (read by the authors as system 1) were rare. This is one session, descriptive.
agent_test: Check whether agent traces that skip expected behaviour (F straight to S) have more errors.

claim: The empirical test of system 1 and system 2 design thinking (Kannengiesser and Gero 2019, Human Behavior in Design) was not obtained; the Design Science 2019 paper is theory only and has no hypotheses or statistics. The H2 outcome (professionals more system 1) is unknown.
agent_test: none

claim: No study was found that (a) compares FBS-labelled agent reasoning with plain chain of thought at equal tokens, (b) forces decomposition-recomposition on an LLM, (c) ablates an expected-vs-derived behaviour check in an LLM design loop, or (d) tests an FBS reformulation step against narrow LLM output spread. The nearest measured analogues are Ma 2024's critique pass and persona line, which raised diversity but stayed below humans. The FMEA review's claim that FBS reduces conceptual errors is unmeasured.
agent_test: Equal-token ablations: plain CoT vs F/Be/Bs/S tags; with and without an evaluation step; with and without a reformulation step; measure spread across 10 seeds.

claim: Held-out multi-coder reliability for LLM coding of FBS design protocols is still missing. Outside design, GPT-4 coding one label per call with a rationale reached kappa 0.68 on 111 gold passages and fell on rare, fuzzy codes; rewording a definition fixed some items and broke others.
agent_test: Have 3 coders and one LLM tag 200 agent-trace segments with F/Be/Bs/S; report kappa per label.
